topic: MCP Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Coordination: What's Coming in H2 2026

key_points: Explains A2A as agent-to-agent teamwork rather than simple tool calling.
Separates A2A roles into client agents that coordinate tasks and remote/service agents that advertise capabilities.
Describes Agent Cards as the discovery/trust mechanism before agents delegate work.
Useful competitive gap: strong conceptual explanation, but light on H2 2026 MCP roadmap changes and production migration guidance.
Positions A2A as an open communication protocol for agents from different vendors and frameworks.
Draws a clear MCP vs A2A distinction: MCP connects agents to APIs, tools, and data; A2A coordinates collaboration between agents.
Lists core A2A components including client, server, Agent Card, task, message, artifact, and part.
Uses a retail inventory/order/supplier example to show MCP and A2A working together.
Frames A2A in a broader 2026 protocol landscape alongside MCP, ACP, ANP, and AP2.
Summarizes A2A flow as discovery, authorization, and communication.
Calls out peer-to-peer delegation, dynamic negotiation, streamed information, and standardized identity.
Competitive gap: broad protocol overview, but less depth on deployment architecture for enterprise agent systems.
Explains A2A as a way for agents from different vendors to discover, delegate, and coordinate tasks.
States that A2A handles agent coordination while MCP handles tool and data access.
Highlights HTTP, SSE, JSON-RPC, Agent Cards, and Tasks as practical A2A building blocks.
Useful angle to expand: A2A compliance alone does not solve shared context, semantic alignment, or governance.

Gives a production-oriented rule of thumb: use MCP when one agent needs structured tool, file, API, or database access; use A2A when multiple autonomous agents need to coordinate long-running work and artifacts.
Frames the two protocols as complementary rather than mutually exclusive.
Notes that 2026 enterprise systems often route tool calls through MCP and reserve A2A for cross-vendor collaboration.
Competitive gap: should be updated with MCP's 2026 release candidate, A2A Linux Foundation adoption milestones, and security lessons.

stats.fact: On April 9, 2026, the Linux Foundation said the A2A protocol had more than 150 supporting organizations, integrations across Google, Microsoft, and AWS platforms, and active production deployments across multiple industries.

The Linux Foundation describes A2A as an open standard for agents to discover, communicate, and transact across frameworks, vendors, and platforms; Google originally developed it and the Linux Foundation now hosts it.

Anthropic reported, when donating MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, that there were more than 10,000 active public MCP servers and adoption across ChatGPT, Cursor, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Visual Studio Code, AWS, Cloudflare, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.

The MCP 2026-07-28 release candidate, announced May 21, 2026, introduces a stateless protocol core, first-class extensions, Tasks, MCP Apps, authorization hardening, formal deprecation policy, and full JSON Schema 2020-12 for tools.

The current MCP specification defines server features for resources, prompts, and tools; client features for sampling, roots, and elicitation; and utilities such as progress tracking, cancellation, error reporting, and logging.

A 2025 arXiv survey of agent interoperability protocols describes MCP as a JSON-RPC client-server interface for secure tool invocation and typed data exchange, while A2A enables peer-to-peer task outsourcing through capability-based Agent Cards.

Cloud Security Alliance research notes that between January and February 2026, researchers and the community filed more than 30 CVEs affecting MCP servers, clients, and infrastructure components; CVE-2025-6514 scored CVSS 9.6 and affected the mcp-remote proxy package across more than 437,000 installed environments.

The public A2A GitHub project page described H2 roadmap items including authorization schemes in Agent Cards, dynamic skill querying, dynamic UX negotiation inside tasks, more client-initiated methods, and better streaming reliability and push notifications.

angles: Layered architecture beats protocol-war framing: MCP is the tool/data access layer, A2A is the coordination layer, and production systems will commonly need both.
H2 2026 is the migration window: MCP's stateless core and Tasks extension change how teams deploy remote MCP servers, long-running agent work, routing, caching, and observability.
A2A's near-term value is not smarter agents by itself; it is standardized discovery, delegation, progress streaming, artifacts, and cross-vendor task handoff.
Agent Cards become an enterprise control point: capability discovery, auth schemes, supported modalities, version negotiation, and policy metadata should be treated like API contracts.
Shared context remains the missing layer: A2A can move tasks between agents, but teams still need definitions, schemas, memory boundaries, evaluation, and semantic alignment.
Security is the adoption tax: MCP tool poisoning, prompt injection, excessive tool scope, agent impersonation, and cross-agent accountability need gateway controls before broad rollout.
The likely winning pattern is an agent gateway: policy enforcement, identity, audit logs, evaluation hooks, MCP server registry, A2A agent registry, and task-level telemetry in one governed layer.
Developers should prototype with one orchestrator, two specialist agents, a narrow MCP server set, explicit task states, and an audit trail before trying open-ended agent marketplaces.
